Terry

> On a side note, would you happen to know of any research concerning which fit indices are applicable to UlS models?

Are you talking about unweighted least squares (ULS) estimation?

> I have been told that RMSEA, CFI, and NNFI are OK. However that SRMR is not. Lavaan produces all fit indices under UlS, although several stats packages do not. Thus I am wondering whether certain fit indices are inappropriate or just that other software not being able to calculate SRMR.

I haven't read any research about fit indices under ULS estimation compared to the same fit indices under MLE, GLS, or WLS.  But I don't see why SRMR couldn't be computed in any software. -- it is just the average standardized difference between observed and model-implied sample moments.  I'm not really a fan of SRMR anyway because a single huge residual should be addressed, even if the average residual is small; thus, I would recommend looking at all standardized residuals.

I have read that ULS estimation should be your last resort because the SEs are so inefficient, and I think the test statistic might over-reject, too (don't quote me on that).  Why are you using ULS instead of a more efficient estimator?

Terry

messages.subject_clean: negative factor loadings in nested factor model: optimizer issue?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I discovered a couple of times negative factor loadings in my nested factor models that should be positive. I thought it might be an issue with starting values / the optimizer / ... . So I looked systematically at the issue and tried to find an reproducible example.

Here it is: Three correlation matrices as input for a nested factor model with a general factor and one specific factor. All factor loadings should be positive.

library(lavaan)

# data input
mat.1 <- structure(c(1, 0.52, 0.52, 0.52, 0.52, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.52, 1, 0.52, 0.52, 0.52, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.52, 0.52, 1, 0.52, 0.52, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.52,
                     0.52, 0.52, 1, 0.52, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.52, 0.52,
                     0.52, 0.52, 1, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.44, 1, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.44, 1, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.44, 1, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.44, 1, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.44, 1), .Dim = c(10L, 10L),
                   .Dimnames = list(c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "a5", "b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5"),
                                    c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "a5", "b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5")))

mat.2 <- structure(c(1, 0.54, 0.54, 0.54, 0.54, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,
                     0.44, 0.54, 1, 0.54, 0.54, 0.54, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44, 0.44,

  g =~ a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5

'

fit.1 <- cfa(mod.nested.factor, sample.cov = mat.1, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.1) # negative factor loadings

fit.2 <- cfa(mod.nested.factor, sample.cov = mat.2, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.2) # positive factor loadings

fit.3 <- cfa(mod.nested.factor, sample.cov = mat.3, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.3) # positive factor loadings

The first model showed negative factor loadings (-0.283) for the specific factor, the other two models showed positive factor loadings. Please note: The pattern is not consistent. Sometimes (after restarting R) some other models has negative factor loadings. I thought providing starting values might solve the issue:

# CFA start values
mod.nested.factor.startvalue <- '
  g =~ a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5
  f1 =~ start(.8)*a1 + start(.8)*a2 + start(.8)*a3 + start(.8)*a4 + start(.8)*a5
'

fit.1.startvalue <- cfa(mod.nested.factor.startvalue, sample.cov = mat.1, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.1.startvalue) # positive factor loadings

fit.2.startvalue <- cfa(mod.nested.factor.startvalue, sample.cov = mat.2, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.2.startvalue) # negative factor loadings

fit.3.startvalue <- cfa(mod.nested.factor.startvalue, sample.cov = mat.3, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.3.startvalue) # positive factor loadings

However, it does not really help. In more complex analysis, different starting values (e.g., .8., .9) change the signs of the factor loadings in an unpredictable matter. It helps to introduce model constraints:

# CFA constraints
mod.nested.factor.constraint <- '
  g =~ a1 + a2 + a3 + a4 + a5 + b1 + b2 + b3 + b4 + b5
  f1 =~ c1*a1 + c2*a2 + c3*a3 + c4*a4 + c5*a5

  c1 > 0
  c2 > 0
  c3 > 0
  c4 > 0
  c5 > 0
'

fit.1.constraint <- cfa(mod.nested.factor.constraint, sample.cov = mat.1, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.1.constraint) # positive factor loadings

fit.2.constraint <- cfa(mod.nested.factor.constraint, sample.cov = mat.2, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.2.constraint) # positive factor loadings

fit.3.constraint <- cfa(mod.nested.factor.constraint, sample.cov = mat.3, sample.nobs = 500, std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
summary(fit.3.constraint) # positive factor loadings

However, that is only a suboptimal solution when you working with real data or more complex models.

Are there any solutions to convince lavaan to use the correct (=positive) factor loadings without constraints or playing around with starting values?

André

Dear All,

I'm trying to replicate Edwards & Lambert (2007)'s empirical example analysis which they did in SPSS and Excel (for God knows what reason). Essentially Z (centrality) moderates every possible link in the model, therefore the name total effect model.

I've been trying to write code using lavaan to fit this model. But I keep getting errors. I really appreciate someone helping me out. Thanks guys! The mean centered data looks like this. Ignore gender for now.

Commitment~b4*Feedback+b5*Centrality+b6*Feedback*Centrality+b7*Satisfaction+ b8*Satisfaction*Centrality

b:= b7+b8*Centrality
ab:= a*b

I don't think this phenomenon is specific to lavaan or any of R's optimizers.  The same thing has happened to me in Mplus, and I'm sure it happens in LISREL, EQS, Amos, etc.  When all of the loadings are in the same direction and the factors are uncorrelated, you get the same model-implied covariance matrix if you just switch the signs:

> lavInspect(fit.1, "cov.ov")
> lavInspect(fit.1.constraint, "cov.ov")

You should get all positive loadings even if you just constrain one of them to be positive.  This phenomenon isn't even specific to bifactor models -- I've seen it happen with regular factor models with simple structure (but switching the sign of factor loadings also switched the sign of that factor's covariance with other factors).  I'm not sure what makes the optimizer search in a different place when the off-diagonal elements in rows/columns 1-5 are < .53 than when they are > .53, and the same thing might not even happen in other software for these specific examples.  But the phenomenon does happen in other software.

If you want to interpret your factor in a specific direction, I don't see why constraining a loading to be positive is suboptimal, but you might also consider posting your question on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> to see if a wider audience has come up with any different solutions.

messages.subject_clean: Replicating Edwards & Lambert (2007)'s Total Effect Model
messages.body_plain:
> A new parameter must be a function of other parameters (which are not themselves new parameters).

User-defined parameters can be functions of other user-defined parameters, such as calculating a total effect from indirect and direct effects:

> set.seed(1234)
> X <- rnorm(100)
> M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
> Y <- 0.7*M + rnorm(100)
> Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)
> model <- ' # direct effect
> Y ~ c*X
> # mediator
> M ~ a*X
> Y ~ b*M
> # indirect effect (a*b)
> ab := a*b
> # total effect
> total := c + ab
> '
> fit <- sem(model, data = Data)
> summary(fit)

But Ed is right that you can't create a user-defined parameter as a function of a variable.  Modeling an interaction requires you to create product terms in your data set and include those as separate variables.  To probe the interaction (i.e., test the indirect effect at different levels of the moderator), you will have to create user-defined parameters for different levels of the moderator.  Hopefully you have specific levels of substantive interest, but if not, you could use the mean and/or 1 SD below and above the mean.  I provided a similar example in an earlier post, in which the moderator was labeled W instead of Z:

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/RW_3TMARGhY/UF9-MBk-GKIJ

You can find it by searching "Moderated mediation" in the search bar.  To test whether the indirect effect is moderated by Z, you can either
run a more-constrained model in which the indirect effects at each level of Z are constrained to be equal (e.g., ' ab0 == ab1 ') and use anova() to compare them, or
create user-defined parameter(s) that are differences between the indirect effects at different levels of Z (e.g., ' ab01 := ab0 - ab1 ')

Hi Sam,

Your question on model fit with a latent interaction model is a relevant one when using a product indicator approach. Product indicator approaches (double mean centering, residual centering), can bias model fit indices (e.g. RMSEA, CFI). Geldhof and colleagues (2013) discuss this issue with residual centering but the issue should also hold in double mean centering applications (short version, in these models the degrees of freedom are incorrect and need to be  corrected). Your syntax looks good, but a couple notes:
Husbands and wives are completing the same items, so the items correlate for 2 reason: (1) the common factors and (2) the item-specific factors. I'm not sure whether you have any missing data, but that is common enough that I'll bring it up just in case.  MLM corrects SEs and test statistics for nonnormality, but only works for complete data.  MLR is asymptotically equivalent but more general, allowing you to use it in conjunction with FIML if you have ignorable missing data.

> fit1b<-sem(model1a, data=data, group = 'Q20', group.equal = c("loadings"))

You don't have any factor loadings to estimate, so this use of the "group.equal" argument doesn't make any sense.  Instead, you want to constrain "regressions".  But using the group.equal argument will not allow you to define the indirect effects you want to estimate.  Instead, you should use the syntax to constrain the parameters to equality, as I suggested in the previous post.  Using only 1 label applies that label to only the first group's parameter, but using a vector of labels allows you to label the parameter in each group.  Assuming you have 2 groups, you could distinguish between parameters of Group 1 using lowercase and Group 2 using uppercase, for example:

> CmMAGm ~ c(a1, A1)*pardis

Note that R is case-sensitive, so "a1" is distinct from "A1", but if you have more groups, you could just give entirely new labels to each group (e.g., 'CmMAGm ~ c(g1.a1, g2.a1, g3.a1)*pardis').  If you give the parameter the same label in both groups, they will be constrained to equality:

> CmMAGm ~ c(a1, a1)*pardis

When the parameters are not constrained to equality across groups, then you define an indirect effect separately for each group, as I showed in my previous post:

> g1.indirect1 := g1.a1 * g1.a2 * g1.a3
> g2.indirect1 := g2.a1 * g2.a2 * g2.a3

 and so on...

> fit1c<-sem(model1a, data=data, group = 'Q20', group.partial = c("mER_total ~~ CmMAGm"))

The group.equal argument is where you provide exceptions to the group.equal argument, so it doesn't make sense to use group.partial without group.equal.  Also, the "~~" operator is for (co)variances, not regressions.  If you want to free one constraint at a time, you need to add the regression parameter you want to free (e.g., 'mER_total ~ CmMAGm').

But again, that would not allow you to define the indirect effect in each group if there are any group differences.  You could use the group.equal shortcut to first find out how many parameters can be constrained across groups (which would not require all the time spent bootstrapping).  Then, once you settle on a model, then you can add the user-defined indirect effects to the syntax.  But you are only working with constraints on 6 regression slopes, so I would suggest you use the lavaan syntax to make your constriants -- it's good practice.

Terry

messages.body_plain:
> I want to control for the influence of the variable "Doku" (just like in a "classical" ANCOVA) while testing for group differences on the dependent variables. Is it correct to regress them onto the variable "Doku"? Compared to a model without the regression, the means are adjusted. Of course, lavaan will estimated the regression coefficients freely across the groups. Is that meaningful? I do have a theoretical justification, but as far as I know this is not done in ANCOVA, right? I think that covariates in ANCOVA should actually be equal across groups...

Yes, you are referring to the "assumption" of homogeneous slopes/hyperplanes in ANCOVA.  In order to test group-differences in adjusted means (or equivalently, group-differences in intercepts in a regression model), the distance between 2 groups' regression lines need to be constant across all levels of the covariate (Doku).  If there is an interaction between Doku and Group, then the lines are not parallel, so group differences are larger at some levels of Doku than at other levels of Doku.  In this case, there is no single valid test of difference in adjusted means or intercepts; instead, you would probe the interaction by testing group-mean differences at multiple meaningful levels of Doku (e.g., the observed minimum, maximum, and median, or the Mean + / - SD, or any levels of Doku that are substantively interesting "subpopulations" to compare).  You do this by centering Doku at each of the chosen levels and running your model(s) again, so that "Doku == 0" represents that centered value.  This works because in the presence of an interaction, the test of a difference in group intercepts (i.e., the effect of Group) is conditional on the moderator (Doku) being held constant at zero.

In the context of a multiple-group CFA/MIMIC model, Group implicitly interacts with every predictor (in your case, Doku and latent factors) because slopes are freely estimated across groups.  In fact, the test of metric (or "weak") invariance is a test of the interaction between Group and the latent factor(s) on the outcomes/indicators.  I will also point out that because you are interested in testing for group-differences in latent intercepts, you need to assume not only that the latent factors are measured invariably across groups, but also that the latent factors are measured invariably across levels of Doku.  If Doku is a continuous variable, you can test invariance using the MIMIC method.  Basically, fit a series of configural-invariance models (i.e., free estimates across groups) in which Doku predicts not only the latent factors but also one indicator per factor, and test whether the effect of Doku on each indicator is zero after controlling for the effect of the latent factor.  You will have to test all indicators, so use a Bonferroni-adjusted alpha level for the number of indicators you test.  If any are significant in either group, include those effects in your configural model when you start to test invariance across groups.  For a valid test of scalar (or "strong") invariance, you will first need to test whether the effects of Doku on any indicators differ across groups (i.e., whether Group and Doku interact in their effects on indicators -- this is testing the assumption of homogenous slopes across groups for the measurement model).  It doesn't matter whether you test the equality of "indicator ~ Doku" effects before or after testing metric invariance, but I would do them in separate steps because they are distinct null hypotheses.  If any Doku effects on indicators exist, and they cannot be constrained across groups, then you have to test partial scalar invariance across groups (i.e., don't constrain intercepts across groups for those indicators).

Back to your original question -- Assuming you have at least partial measurement invariance with respect to Group and to Doku, then you need to test whether the effects of Doku on latent factors are equal across groups.  If none differ, then there is no evidence of an interaction, so you can finally test group-differences in latent intercepts while controlling for Doku (same as testing group-differences in adjusted means in ANCOVA).  However, if any effects of Doku on latent variables differ across groups, then you would need to probe the Group-Doku interaction by testing group-mean differences at some meaningful levels of Doku (use centering, as described in the first paragraph).

Good luck,

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

So you are running a multiple-group model, where the different age cohorts are the different groups, but every cohort has a fixed schedule?  This is way simpler than defining a different schedule for each individual, as Mehta & Neale were describing (which is not available in lavaan).  You are fitting the same model in each group, but you are just fixing the loadings to different time-values in each group.  See the lavaan tutorial for how to do this:  http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

> age 3 group:
> s =~ 0*mdss1 + 0.3*mdss2 + 0.8*mdss3 + 1.2*mdss4 + 1.8*mdss5
>
> age 6 group:
> s =~ 0.3*mdss1 + 0.8*mdss2 + 1.2*mdss3 + 1.8*mdss4 + 2.1*mdss5
>
> age 9 group:
> s =~ 0.8*mdss1 + 1.2*mdss2 + 1.8*mdss3 + 2.1*mdss4 + 2.4*mdss5
>

Assuming these are the only three groups, it would look like this:

And you can easily extrapolate to more age cohorts by putting more fixed values in the vectors.

What is an "overall'' solution?  Every group will have their own estimates of the mean and variance of the linear slope.  If you want to see whether the slope is the same across groups, then you can constrain that parameter to equality by using the same label across the 6 cohorts:

Well, you are currently defining the "interac" parameter as a function of other parameters.  The slope of an interaction term is not a function of other parameters; rather, you estimate the slope of an interaction like you would the slopes of any other predictors, but the slope of an interaction will be the effect of the product of the predictors that interact.  In other functions like lm() and glm() that accept formula objects, you can just specify interactions by using the asterisk or colon operators in the formula, but lavaan syntax does not work that way.  You would have to calculate product terms yourself as new variables in your data set, then regress the outcome(s) on those variable names in your model syntax.  You can search topics for "interaction" or "moderation" to see other examples in previous posts in this group.

This is a strange scenario because you have a formative construct.  The only way I can think to get this done is to consider the statistically equivalent model in which X is measured reflectively by W, and the Ys are simply exogenous predictors.   Because X would be a single indicator construct in that perspective (which is statistically indistinguishable from your theory), you don't need X at all.  You could just model the effects of the Ys and the Zs directly on W, and estimate the interactions between the Ys and Zs by calculating their products as new variables in your data set, then including those products as predictors in your model syntax.

There are others who work more with formative constructs and PLS software than I do, and they might have better suggestions.  Consider posting on SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>, too.  I think this might be a curiosity regardless of the SEM software you use, and there is a larger audience there.

Dear Ulrich,

The groups labeled "1" and "2" are not necessarily sexes 1 and 2 in your data set.  Read about the "group.label" argument in the ?lavaan help page.  When the first group is sex "2" instead of sex "1", that affects which group's latent-response scales/residual variances are fixed vs. estimated (given that the loadings and thresholds are constrained to equality), as well as the sign of the latent mean-differences.  You will get consistent results when you use this argument:  fit.3dim <- cfa(..., group.label = c("1","2"), ...)

I noticed in your script you were saving the standardized means in group 2.  Like you, I would also expect them to be the same (with opposite sign) if all that changes is which sex is called "group 1", especially given that the fit measures match to so many decimal places.  But things get complicated with binary data.  A change in observed cell counts can be modeled equivalently either as a change in thresholds or a change in variance of the latent item-response, so I'm not sure whether the optimizer simply settles in a slightly different local maximum that happens to yield the same log-likelihood.  If you look at the output of lavInspect(fit.3dim, "cov.ov") when using sex 1 as either the first or second group, you will notice the model-implied polychoric correlations are the same, but the output of lavInspect(fit.3dim, "mean.ov") do not merely change signs in the second group's model-implied means (first group is a zero vector).  But there is no bug in how the standardized values are calculated.  If you calculate the standardized latent mean difference from the parameterEstimates() output (group 2 mean divided by the square-root of group 2 variance), you get what you see in the standardizeSolution() output.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> Can I know how to mediation effect calculation in the 'blavaan' library?

The same way you would in lavaan.  blavaan translates lavaan model syntax into a jags syntax file, then runs it.  Adapting the example from the lavaan tutorial page: http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

> set.seed(1234)

> M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
> Y <- 0.7*M + rnorm(100)
> Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)

>              Y ~ c*X
>            # mediator
>              M ~ a*X
>              Y ~ b*M
>            # indirect effect (a*b)
>              ab := a*b
>            # total effect
>              total := c + (a*b)
>          '
>
> fit <- bsem(model, data = Data, # jagcontrol=list(method="rjparallel"),
>             n.chains = 3, burnin = 1000, sample = 1000,
>             jagfile = "path/to/directory")

Notice in the summary() output that there is no prior or PSRF for the defined parameters because they are just calculated from other model parameters.  Instead of using the delta method to calculate normal-theory-based SEs, you just use the M and SD (or credible interval) of the posterior distribution to make an inference (like you would if you bootstrapped SEs or CIs).

> is it that you are using `s` that indicates that this is the latent variance of the slope?

I used "s" because you used "s".  That is the name of the variable in your model syntax that is the latent slope.  Its variance is defined using the usual lavaan syntax rules <http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html>.

> What if I wanted to constrain the latent slope parameter itself?

The latent slope is not a fixed parameter.  It is a variable, which has parameters that you can estimate or fix, such as a mean ('s ~ 1') and variance ('s ~~ s').  It is a variable because every case (row) has a different rate of change: the mean of "s" is the average of all the individual slopes.  If you want to force every case to have the same slope, you can fix the variance to zero ('s ~~ c(0, 0)*s'), which would make it a constant slope, implying it cannot covary with the latent intercept ('s ~~ c(0, 0)*i').

> What that be `i`?

No, that is a different variable (the latent intercept).  You might want to search for some introductions to growth curve modeling to read (e.g., the first half of ALDA <http://gseacademic.harvard.edu/~alda/>, with chapter 8 focusing on the SEM framework; or Preacher et al.'s booklet <http://www.amazon.com/Latent-Modeling-Quantitative-Applications-Sciences/dp/1412939550>).

What is the difference between these facets?  They have the same 3 indicators, and Facet 1 has an additional 4th indicator.  That does not seem like enough to identify them as unique factors, so I think the only reason this model even converges on a solution is because you set "orthogonal = TRUE" (which contradicts the covariance between facets in your diagram). The product-indicator approach only works for defining first-order constructs (because you would need to calculate products among observed variables, not latent variables). You can add the error term in a couple of ways. First, you can define the formative LV and then free its error variance

F <~ x1 + x2 + x3

Alternatively, you can just define a latent variable without indicators and regress it on the x’s

F =~ 0
F ~ x1 + x2 + x3

I prefer the latter syntax because it is more difficult to unintentionally specify a composite model with this syntax. Note that in both specifications you may need to manually fix some of the parameters to known non-zero values to identify the model.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, experts!

I'm trying to fit a bifactor model to a reasonably large set of complete data (N = 445).  The following is the initial proposed bifactor model:

> measurement.model3 <- "attitude =~ FSE11 + FSE14 + FSE15 + HO4 + HO5 + ISCO3 + ISCU4 + STR2 + STR3
>                        self.efficacy =~ FSE13 + FSE16 + FSE2 + FSE6 + FSE7 + FSE8 + ISCO1 + ISMP5 + ISSH5 + FSE3 + ISCO5 + ISMP2 + ISMP3 + ISMP7 + ISSH4 + ISCO2 + ISMP6
>                       structure =~ FSE11 + FSE14 + FSE15 + HO4 + HO5 + ISCO3 + ISCU4 + STR2 + STR3 + FSE13 + FSE16 + FSE2 + FSE6 + FSE7 + FSE8 + ISCO1 + ISMP5 + ISSH5 + FSE3 + ISCO5 + ISMP2 + ISMP3 + ISMP7 + ISSH4 + ISCO2 + ISMP6
>                       # HO4 ~~ HO5
>                       attitude ~~ self.efficacy
>                       structure ~~ 0*attitude + 0*self.efficacy
>                       "

That is: the general factor (called "structure" here) is theorized to affect indicators but not the specific factors.  When I submit this model to a "standard" CFA I get the following results:

>  lavaan (0.5-20) converged normally after 852 iterations
>   Number of observations                           445
>   Estimator                                         ML
>   Minimum Function Test Statistic              715.942
>   Degrees of freedom                               272
>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000
> Warning message:
> In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
>   lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!
>   lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified.

In reading the message boards here I feel like it's implied that for a bifactor model to be identified the specific factors must be specified as uncorrelated with each other, as well as the general factor.  Is this the case?  That doesn't seem to be how bifactor models are described in the literature (e.g., Kline 2016 p320), but I am certainly no expert.  If it's not the case, what are the criteria for identifying a bifactor model?  It seems like it should be good to go.

As a followup, I am hoping to eventually add causal indicators to the structure factor, which obviously will be a problem if the model is already underidentified..

Thanks!
Jake

On 04/28/2016 04:00 PM, kais...@stud.sbg.ac.at wrote:
> Variances:
> EstimateStd.Err Z-value  P(>|z|)

>      v1 0.3500.1212.8980.004
>      v2 0.4730.1213.9240.000
>      etc.
> |
> How can I extract these values from the object?

You can't. The summary() function is for display only. If you need to
extract values, please use the parameterEstimates() function. This
returns a data.frame, which you can filter in the usual way.

For example:

library(lavaan)
example(cfa)

# all rows with variances
PE[ PE$op == "~~" & PE$lhs == PE$rhs, ]

# all variance estimates
PE[ PE$op == "~~" & PE$lhs == PE$rhs, "est"]

# observed (residual) variances only:
PE[ PE$op == "~~" & PE$lhs == PE$rhs & PE$lhs %in% lavNames(PE, "ov"),
"est"]

# latent variances only:
PE[ PE$op == "~~" & PE$lhs == PE$rhs & PE$lhs %in% lavNames(PE, "lv"),
"est"]

Yves.

Your description is mostly confusing (I can't tell what "2-5" or "5-9" mean), but I notice from your picture that your sample size is only 29. SEM is a large-sample technique, and its statistics are based on asymptotic theory, so I doubt you will be able to fit a model to this sample without some kind of errors.

lavaan does not have an "na.omit" argument, but it has a "missing" argument that you could set to "pairwise" so that lavaan will calculate polychoric correlations using all available information.  You can look at the help pages for ?factor and ?levels to see how to control the levels of your factors -- it looks like you might need to get rid of empty categories (the error message has nothing to do with missing values, which lavaan ignores by default by setting missing = "listwise").
